t: Maximum Binary Tree II — Appending a Value to a Maximum Tree
o: We are given the maximum tree built from an array `a`, but not `a` itself. We must return the tree that would result from appending `val` to the end of `a` and rebuilding. The key observation is that appending only affects the rightmost path of the tree: the new element can never become the left child of anything, and it only competes with nodes on the path of right children. In Example 1, `val = 5` is larger than every node, so it becomes the new root with the old tree as its left child. In Example 2, `val = 3` is smaller than root 5 but larger than node 4's subtree values along the right spine, so it becomes the right child of 5 and node 4 becomes its left child. In Example 3, `val = 4` is smaller than 5 but larger than 3, so it replaces 3 as the right child of 5, with 3 as its left child. With at most 100 nodes, even a brute-force reconstruction works, but a single walk down the right spine gives an elegant $O(h)$ solution.
k: Appending to the array only modifies the chain of right children (the right spine) of the existing tree.
If `val` exceeds all values on the right spine, it becomes the new root; otherwise it is inserted at the first node whose value is smaller.
The inserted node always takes the displaced subtree as its left child, since the appended element sits after everything in the original array.

a.n: Approach 1: Reconstruct from inorder traversal (brute force)
a.i: An inorder traversal of a maximum tree recovers the original array `a` exactly, because Construct recursively places left elements before the root and right elements after. Once we have `a`, append `val` and rebuild the maximum tree using a monotonic stack in linear time. This is the most direct translation of the problem statement into code.
s: Inorder-traverse the given tree to recover array `a`.
Rebuild using a monotonic stack: for each value, pop stack nodes with smaller values; the last popped becomes the left child, and the top of the stack (if any) gets the new node as its right child.
Push the new node and return the bottom-of-stack root.
a.t: O(n) — one traversal plus one linear stack-based rebuild.
a.sp: O(n) — the recovered array and the stack.

a.n: Approach 2: Recursive insertion on the right spine (optimal)
a.i: Since `val` is appended at the end of the array, it must appear after every original element. Therefore it can only be placed along the right spine: walk down right children until we find a node whose value is less than `val`. At that point, `val` becomes the new root of this subtree, the old subtree becomes its left child, and the parent keeps pointing to the new node. If no such node exists, `val` becomes the overall new root.
s: If root is null or root.val < val, create a node with val whose left child is root and return it.
Otherwise, recursively insert val into root.right.
a.t: O(h) where h is the height of the tree — we only descend the right spine; O(n) worst case for a skewed tree.
a.sp: O(h) recursion depth; O(1) extra space iteratively.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force rebuild briefly, then present the recursive right-spine insertion as the optimal answer — it is three lines per language and shows you understand the structure of maximum trees. Common pitfalls: forgetting to attach the old subtree as the *left* child of the inserted node (it must be left, not right, because the appended element comes after all original elements); comparing with `<` vs `<=` (values are unique so either works, but `<` is conventional). Edge cases: `val` larger than the root (new root returned), a single-node tree, and inserting into a fully right-skewed tree (worst-case O(n)). Follow-ups: how would you handle multiple insertions (repeatedly apply, amortized fine), or deletion of the last element (undo the last insertion by searching the right spine)?
